{{Short description|Statistical rule of thumb}}

'''Sturges's rule'''<ref name=sturges>{{cite journal |last=Sturges |first=H. A. |year=1926 |title=The choice of a class interval |journal=Journal of the American Statistical Association |volume=21 |issue=153 | pages=65–66 | jstor=2965501 | doi = 10.1080/01621459.1926.10502161 }}</ref> is a method to choose the number of bins for a [[histogram]]. Given <math>n</math> observations, Sturges's rule suggests using 

:<math>
\hat{k} = 1 + \log_2(n)
</math>

bins in the histogram. This rule is widely employed in [[data analysis]] software including [[Python (programming language)|Python]]<ref>{{cite web | url=https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.histogram_bin_edges.html#numpy.histogram_bin_edges | title=Numpy.histogram_bin_edges — NumPy v2.1 Manual }}</ref> and [[R (programming language)|R]], where it is the default bin selection method.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/graphics/versions/3.6.2/topics/hist | title=Hist function - RDocumentation }}</ref>

Sturges's rule comes from the [[binomial distribution]] which is used as a discrete approximation to the [[normal distribution]].<ref name="Scott2009WIRE">{{cite journal|last=Scott|first=David W.|title=Sturges' rule|journal = WIREs Computational Statistics|volume=1|issue=3|year=2009|pages=303–306 |doi=10.1002/wics.35|s2cid=197483064 }}</ref> If the function to be approximated <math>f</math> is binomially distributed then 
:<math>
f(y) = \binom{m}{y} p^y (1-p)^{m-y}
</math>
where <math>m</math> is the number of trials and <math>p</math> is the probability of success and <math>y = 0,1,\ldots,m</math>. Choosing <math>p=1/2</math> gives
:<math>
f(y) = \binom{m}{y} 2^{-m}
</math>
In this form we can consider <math>2^{-m}</math> as the normalisation factor and Sturges's rule is saying that the sample should result in a histogram with bin counts given by the [[binomial coefficients]]. Since the total sample size is fixed to <math>n</math> we must have
:<math>
n = \sum_y \binom{m}{y} = 2^m
</math>
using the well-known formula for [[binomial coefficient#Sums of the binomial coefficients|sums of the binomial coefficients]]. Solving this by taking logs of both sides gives <math>m = \log_2(n)</math> and finally using <math>k = m+1</math> (due to counting the 0 outcomes) gives Sturges's rule. In general Sturges's rule does not give an integer answer so the result is rounded up.

==Doane's formula==

Doane<ref name=Doane1976>Doane DP (1976) Aesthetic frequency classification. American Statistician, 30: 181–183</ref> proposed modifying Sturges's formula to add extra bins when the data are [[Skewness|skewed]]. Using the [[Method of moments (statistics)|method of moments]] estimator
: <math>
    g_1 = \frac{m_3}{m_2^{3/2}}
        = \frac{\tfrac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\overline{x})^3}{\left[\tfrac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\overline{x})^2 \right]^{3/2}},
  </math>
along with its variance
:<math> \sigma_{g_1}^2= \frac { 6(n-2) }{ (n+1)(n+3) }</math>

Doane proposed adding <math>
\log_2 \left( 1 +  \frac { |g_1| }{\sigma_{g_1}} \right)
</math> extra bins giving ''Doane's formula''
:<math>
\hat{k} = 1 + \log_2(n) + \log_2 \left( 1 +  \frac { |g_1| }{\sigma_{g_1}} \right)
</math>
For symmetric distributions <math>|g_1| \simeq 0</math> this is equivalent to Sturges's rule. For asymmetric distributions a number of additional bins will be used. 

== Criticisms ==

[[File:Histogram log rules.png|thumb|Histogram of 10,000 samples from a [[Gamma distribution|Gamma]](2,2) distribution. Number of bins suggested by [[Scott's rule]] is 61, Doane's rule 21, and Sturges's rule 15.]]

Sturges's rule is not based on any sort of optimisation procedure, like the [[Freedman–Diaconis rule]] or [[Scott's rule]]. It is simply posited based on the approximation of a normal curve by a binomial distribution. [[Rob J. Hyndman|Hyndman]] has pointed out<ref>Hyndman RJ. The problem with Sturges' rule for constructing histograms. Monash University. 1995 Jul 5:1-2.</ref> that any multiple of the binomial coefficients would also converge to a normal distribution, so any number of bins could be obtained following the derivation above. Scott<ref name="Scott2009WIRE" /> shows that Sturges's rule in general produces oversmoothed histograms i.e. too few bins, and advises against its use in favour of other rules such as Freedman-Diaconis or Scott's rule.
